issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: 'Talking about the future' is a weak and atypical trigger for a life-threatening accident in this profile, and it lacks a clear clinical link to the rest of the selected memory, threat, and appraisal items. The other triggers are interpersonal/victim-related, but this item suggests a different theme that is not supported elsewhere.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'Checking if someone is following me' implies pursuit/interpersonal threat. In a life-threatening accident profile, this is hard to reconcile with the rest of the report, which otherwise reflects generalized danger, hypervigilance, and trauma-memory disturbance rather than a specific persecutory/following threat.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: For a 58-year-old fisherman with a life-threatening accident, 'Reminders of victims' implies exposure to multiple casualties or dead/injured others. That is not impossible, but it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise reads like a personal survival-focused accident trauma rather than a mass-casualty/witnessing-victims presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by disorganized, present-tense reliving ('Cannot Find Words', 'Feels Present Not Past'), which fits severe PTSD, but 'intense rage' on recall points to a qualitatively different emotional tone that is not supported elsewhere by the triggers, threat, or appraisals. With no corroborating anger/blame themes, this item stands out as internally and cross-node incongruent.

vignette:
Ravi Patel was 58 when he came to treatment, a widowed South Asian fisherman who had spent most of his life on the water and now found that even ordinary days in the harbor felt altered. The accident that changed him had happened during a storm surge, when his boat was struck hard and he was thrown against the deck, believing for a few terrifying minutes that he would not make it back. He could still describe the wet metal, the shouting, and the way the boat lurched, but when he tried to tell the story in full he said the words would not come. He knew what happened, yet the memory arrived in fragments that felt present rather than past, as if he were still pinned in that moment, and each recollection brought back the same terror that had seized him on the water. In those early weeks he began to notice that talk of people losing loved ones, or even a stranger asking him an ordinary question at the dock, pulled him back into that scene with force. A brief conversation about a neighbor’s funeral could leave him staring past the speaker, feeling the deck beneath him and the storm in his chest all over again, and a chance interaction with someone he did not know could make his mind jump straight to the accident.

As the memory stayed vivid and wordless, Ravi came to believe that people were not what they seemed. The storm had shown him how quickly things could turn dangerous, and he began to mistrust the world around him as though hidden harm might be waiting beneath any calm surface. He also found himself saying that he did not know himself anymore, as if the man who had once handled rough seas without hesitation had been replaced by someone brittle and unfamiliar, and he no longer trusted his own body to hold steady when it mattered. Those beliefs did not remain abstract; they deepened each time he was reminded of the accident by the same kinds of cues that first set him off. A television image of a car hit by an accident could make his pulse race and his recollection sharpen into something immediate and unbearable, and hearing a story of loss could bring the scene back with such force that he again felt the shock in his chest and the helplessness in his limbs. Once the memory surged, his sense that he could not trust himself or others grew stronger, and in turn the accident felt closer, less finished, more ready to return.

By the time he sought help, Ravi had become constantly alert in ways that exhausted him. He felt on guard even inside his own home, especially when the house was unexpectedly quiet, because unusual silence seemed to him like the warning sign before something dangerous. He said that stillness made him scan the room, the doors, the windows, and the sounds outside, looking for any hint that trouble was about to break through. That scanning had begun to shape where he could and could not go. At the fish market he avoided talking to strangers when he could, and if someone unfamiliar approached him to ask about his catch, he would answer quickly and move away. He also steered clear of conversations about bereavement and accidents, because he knew they could throw him back into the memory and leave him shaken for hours. The more he watched for danger, the more certain he became that danger was there, and the more his body felt untrustworthy, as if it might fail him without warning. That fear made him search even harder for signs of threat, and the searching itself kept him primed for the next reminder — a sudden silence in the house, a stranger’s voice, a passing car with a crumpled side — any of which could pull the accident back into the room with him.

Ravi finally came for help after realizing that these reactions were no longer confined to the harbor or the storm season; they were following him into his home, stealing his sleep and narrowing his life. He was most afraid that he would keep losing himself to the same terror and that another sudden moment of danger would catch him unprepared. At the same time, he admitted that he was hoping treatment might help him feel like himself again and make the world seem less like a place where anything calm could turn deadly.
